li.a: Adalah: Uprooted Palestinians Demand to End Desecration of Mass Graves in the Destroyed Village of Tantura, Site of 1948 Massacre
Tablet Magazine: In 2000, a Newspaper Headline Opened a Wound in Israeli Society. It Still Hasn't Healed.
The Guardian: UK study of 1948 Israeli massacre of Palestinian village reveals mass grave sites
Arab News: 3 possible mass graves identified in former Palestinian village
Jewish Telegraphic Agency: Explosive new Israeli documentary 'Tantura' is prompting calls to excavate a possible Palestinian mass grave
Times Higher Education: Eyewitness: Tantura - the village with no future

content.p: On the night of 22 to 23 May 1948, seven days after Israel had declared itself a state, units of the Alexandroni Brigade attacked and occupied Tantura, a Palestinian fishing village of about 1,500 people on the Mediterranean coast near Haifa. Survivors have described what followed as the killing of men who had surrendered, and some veterans of the brigade have described a massacre in a 2022 film. How many died, who gave the orders and whether the killings took place as described have been argued in Israel for more than twenty years, and the argument has returned again and again to the courts, university committees and the cinema.
content.h2: A fishing village on the coast
content.p: Tantura lay within the area that the UN partition resolution had assigned to the future Jewish state, according to Times Higher Education. Most of its residents relied on agriculture and fishing, and Adalah, a legal rights group, describes it as a village of about 1,500 people before the attack. The Guardian describes it as a fishing village of approximately 1,500 people near Haifa.

After the occupation the village was emptied and destroyed. Adalah says about 1,200 survivors were forced from their homes. Some were sent to the nearby village of Fureidis, while others went to neighboring Arab countries. The Guardian places the wider upheaval of 1948 at about 700,000 people expelled or fleeing, and about 500 villages destroyed. Arab News gives a higher figure for the same upheaval, 750,000 people, and says at least 500 Palestinian towns and villages were destroyed. The two outlets give different numbers for the same event, and both are shown here as reported.

According to Adalah, the Alexandroni Brigade of the Haganah attacked and occupied the village during the night of 22 to 23 May. Times Higher Education names the unit as the Third Battalion of the Israeli army's Alexandroni Brigade. The two accounts agree on the brigade and the date.

The accounts diverge on what happened next. Adalah says that testimony from Palestinian survivors, testimony from veterans of the brigade, and official documents from the Israeli army archives show that a systematic massacre of disarmed fighters and civilians took place in the hours after the village was occupied. Adalah puts the number killed at about 280, most of them men. According to the Guardian, survivors and historians have for a long time asserted that men in Tantura were shot after giving themselves up to the brigade, and that the bodies ended up in a mass grave. Estimates in that account have ranged from 40 to 200 people. Arab News reports the same survivor accounts as suggesting that up to 200 men may have been executed after surrendering.

Those figures come from parties with a stake in the outcome. Adalah, a Palestinian-run human rights group, acted for the displaced families, so its figure is their advocates' estimate. The figures are presented here with their sources, not as settled findings.
content.h2: A thesis, a headline and a lawsuit
content.p: The controversy began with a master's student. Teddy Katz, a student at Haifa University, submitted a thesis in March 1998 on the departure of Arab residents from villages at the southern foothills of Carmel in 1948. Tablet reports that the thesis, about 150 pages long and built on interviews Katz had gathered over several years from former residents of Tantura, received top marks of 97. Professors, Tablet says, regard that as possibly the best grade the university has ever given a thesis. The thesis was then shelved.

It came back into public view in January 2000. The weekend edition of the newspaper Maariv, on 21 January 2000, ran a headline reading "The Massacre in Tantura!" over an article by Amir Gilat, who was also a student at Haifa University. According to Tablet, the article described shootings in the streets, in houses and, in groups of six to ten, at the village cemetery, and said that more than 200 non-combatants had been killed. Times Higher Education says that Katz's interviews with witnesses on both sides pointed to as many as 150 people from Tantura, largely unarmed young men, being shot once the village had given up. Afterwards its population was dispersed and the village was destroyed.

Veterans of the Alexandroni Brigade responded with a libel suit against Katz, claiming 1.1 million shekels, about $300,000, in damages. Tablet reports that the veterans' lawyer showed several errors in the thesis during the trial. Some were serious, including quotations that did not match the transcripts of the taped interviews. Katz's lawyers did not present a defence, because Katz began to suffer an aneurysm during the proceedings, and he settled outside court. Tablet reports that Katz settled, or was pressured to settle, depending on whom one believes.
content.h2: The university inquiry and the disputed quotations
content.p: Haifa University set up an internal committee to re-examine the thesis. According to Times Higher Education, its members re-read the work and agreed that Katz had fabricated quotes. Katz disputed the finding. He said, "Of the 144 quotes in the section on Tantura, (only) three were inexact," and said the committee had not told him to correct the work, but had aimed to show that justice lay with the Alexandroni Brigade.

The head of the university's Middle Eastern history department, Avner Giladi, gave a more qualified view. He told Times Higher Education that the committee did not deny that something wrong had happened at Tantura. He acknowledged "methodological problems where summaries are presented as quotations," but said there was no real dispute between the content of the interviews and Katz's paraphrases. He added that if the committee could not say there had been intended falsification, the rest was open to academic debate.

The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reports that Katz signed a statement recanting his research and then said that the statement had been coerced. The university withdrew the thesis from its shelves. Tablet notes that Katz later suffered a second aneurysm and a stroke, and that he received threats after the trial. Tablet describes the case as a left-right dispute, and quotes the peace activist Uri Avnery as saying that the fight was less about 1948 than about the politics of the present. Both points are reported as the views of the people quoted.
content.h2: Mass graves beneath a car park
content.p: The question of where the dead were buried moved from testimony to mapping in 2023. Forensic Architecture, a research agency at Goldsmiths, University of London, analysed British Mandate-era maps and aerial photographs, together with archival records, eyewitness testimony and Israeli army records. It used the material to build a three-dimensional model of the village and to estimate where executions and mass graves may lie, and where the old cemeteries stood. The research was commissioned by Adalah.

The Guardian reports that the investigation identified three possible mass graves beneath a present-day beach resort. The earlier-known grave is placed in open ground beside cacti and three trees, and is now thought to lie under a car park for Dor Beach. A second site, in an orchard near where the village square used to be, is believed to be under concrete, also beneath a car park. Aerial photographs show both as long, thin earth features. A third site, a courtyard behind a house of the Haj Yahya family, is considered a possible execution site, and human bones were reportedly found there years later. Arab News describes the same three locations as potential sites, and says the third had human remains recovered from it several years later. Adalah's own letter, dated 24 May 2023, speaks of four mass graves and the village's cemeteries. The two counts differ, and the sources do not explain the difference.

According to the Guardian, the earlier-known grave has not been exhumed or excavated. A survivor who was 17 when Tantura fell has described, in academic and press accounts, how soldiers made him and a friend dig a grave, into which dozens of bodies were then thrown. The Guardian quotes him as saying, "I will never forget that day, it's still very clear to me. I lost my belief in God that day." Suhad Bishara, Adalah's legal director, said, "It is hard to argue that there are no mass graves in Tantura." Bishara also said that the families' rights to visit the sites and to a dignified burial had "obviously been violated under both Israeli and international law."

Adalah then filed a petition in Israel on behalf of several families who still live in the country, asking for the sites to be marked. Bishara said the aim was not a ruling on whether graves existed but a decision on how to give families access to them.
content.h2: A film and renewed calls for excavation
content.p: The subject returned to Israeli public debate in January 2022, when "Tantura," a documentary by the filmmaker Alon Schwarz, premiered virtually at the Sundance Film Festival on 20 January. The film interviews several veterans of the Alexandroni Brigade, many of them in their nineties, four of whom have lived on Kibbutz Nahsholim since 1948. JTA quotes one of them as saying, "We killed them. No qualms at all." Another said he "didn't count" how many unarmed Palestinians he killed. Accounts within the film put the toll between 200 and 300, JTA reports.

JTA reports that the Palestinian Authority and the editorial board of the newspaper Haaretz called for a commission to dig up land near Mount Carmel in search of an alleged mass grave, in which perhaps 300 Palestinians may be buried. The Palestinian Authority said an international commission should look into the claims in the film. JTA also records that the film includes Ilan Pappe, the historian who had been a major supporter of Katz's thesis, and that IDF historian Yoav Gelber criticised Katz's reliance on oral testimony. In the film, Gelber says, "I don't believe witnesses."

JTA notes that the film does not explain why the veterans chose to speak again. The director suggests they opened up "as if they wanted to share a truth deep inside their soul." JTA also reports that Katz himself warns the director in the film that people who make a film from the taped testimony could be hunted down, as Katz had been.

The figures in the sources do not agree. The Guardian gives a range of 40 to 200 people. Arab News reports survivor accounts of up to 200 men. Katz's research, as Times Higher Education reports it, suggested up to 150 mostly unarmed young men shot after the surrender. Adalah estimates about 280 dead. The film, as JTA describes it, puts the toll at 200 to 300. Maariv's 2000 headline and article spoke of more than 200 non-combatants. Each figure belongs to the person or outlet that gave it, and none has been confirmed by an excavation.

What the sources agree on is narrower. The village was attacked and occupied in the night of 22 to 23 May 1948 by the Alexandroni Brigade. It was emptied of its residents, and its houses were destroyed. Survivors say men who had surrendered were killed, and veterans interviewed in the 2022 film describe a massacre. A 2023 study by Forensic Architecture identified possible mass graves that remain unexcavated. The university committee concluded that Katz had fabricated quotations in his thesis, while Katz said only three of 144 quotations in the Tantura section were inexact. The libel case ended in an out-of-court settlement, according to Tablet. Whether mass graves exist beneath the car park at Dor Beach remains untested.
